The Ephesian Widows (Part 5)

  • August 14, 2026
  • 1 Timothy 3, All Posts on Equality, Church History, Early Church Women, Paul and Women, Women in Ministry
  • 1 Timothy 5, Celibacy, Ephesian Widows, Patronage, Widows, Women in Church History

Female Patrons of Virgins and Widows

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 16:17
Instaread

In part 5 of my series, I look at the last verse, verse 16, in Paul’s discussion of the Ephesian widows in 1 Timothy 5, where he mentions female patrons of widows.

« Part 1. The Different Kinds of Widows in Ephesus
« Part 2. Ordinary Widows and Enrolled Widows
« Part 3. Official Widows in Early Church Documents
« Part 4. Younger Women Who Chose to Stay Single

Introduction

Paul did not want the church to be responsible for the care of the single women in Ephesus. It seems there were so many of them that it could have become a considerable financial and administrative burden for the church. But in 1 Timothy 5:16, he briefly refers to another avenue of support.

Previously in 1 Timothy 5, Paul said that genuine widows should be cared for by their children and grandchildren, their blood relatives. The type of woman mentioned in verse 16 was not usually a blood relative of widows. Rather, she was a patron of single, celibate women.[1] She may even have overseen a group home for them.

Unfortunately, this idea of a patroness is not reflected in English translations of 1 Timothy 5:16a that have added the words “relatives” (e.g., ESV, NLT, NRSV), “in her family” (e.g., CEB, CSB, GNT, NET), or “dependent” (e.g., NASB) in this verse. Adding these words reflects the translators’ interpretation of 1 Timothy 5:16, rather than the underlying Greek text.

The ESV, for example, has,

“If any believing woman has relatives who are widows, let her care for them. Let the church not be burdened …”

The NIV does a better job with,

“If any woman who is a believer has widows in her care, she should continue to help them and not let the church be burdened with them …”

It seems that Paul wanted female patrons to take responsibility for the women who had rejected marriage, so that the church could help the ordinary, genuine widows (ontōs chēras) who had no family (5:16b). The church would also support the enrolled senior Widows who served the church in an official capacity.

Female Patrons of Widows and Virgins

Widows and never-married celibate women in the early church were often cared for by female benefactors.[2] Young women who converted to Christianity in defiance of their family, especially women who also rejected marriage, as well as poor widows, needed the help and protection of the church or of wealthy patrons.[3]

Tabitha in Joppa

Tabitha, also known as Dorcas, is described in Acts 9:36 as a disciple who “was always doing good works and acts of charity” (CSB). It’s often understood that Tabitha made clothes for widows, but her ministry involved much more. It seems she had taken responsibility for caring for a group of widows and she may even have housed them in her own home. The setting of Acts 9:39-41 appears to be Tabitha’s home. Acts 9 shows that the church in Joppa valued the ministry of Tabitha and that she was held in high esteem. She wasn’t a seamstress sewing one garment at a time on her own.[4]

The widows in Joppa are mentioned as a group in Acts 9:39 (“all the widows”) and also in Acts 9:41, where Peter calls “the saints and the widows.” Bonnie Thurston writes that these two phrases in Acts 9 indicate that widows “may already have been a special class” and that they “were a recognizable group within the Christian community.”[5] Some of the widows who Tabitha cared for may have been young, never-married women.

I’ve written more about Tabitha here.

Gavia in Smyrna

At the beginning of the second century, Ignatius closed his letter to the Smyrnaeans and greeted “the virgins who are called widows” (Ign. Smyrn. 13.1). The congregation at Smyrna, roughly 60 kms north of Ephesus, included a group of women who had chosen to remain celibate. The next people Ignatius greets in his letter are the household of a woman named Gavia: “I greet the household of Gavia, and pray that she may be firmly grounded in faith and love both physically and spiritually” (Ign. Smyrn. 13:2).

Christine Trevett believes that Gavia being greeted immediately after the widows “prompts the speculation that she was a (or the) benefactress of such celibate Christian women in Smyrna.”[6] Trevett also suggests that Gavia “was probably a female presbyter [elder] with episkopos (that is, oversight) responsibilities” (cf. Hermas Sim. 9.27.2).[7]

Proba in Rome

It is not certain if Tabitha and Gavia housed widows,[8] but the evidence for such patronesses picks up and becomes clearer in later early church writings. In part 3, I mentioned Marcella and Macrina the Younger who each accommodated groups of widows and virgins in their large homes and educated them.

In 412, admittedly more than 300 years after 1 Timothy was written, Augustine wrote a lengthy letter to a widow named Anicia Faltonia Proba on the subject of prayer. Proba belonged to the aristocratic Anicii family and was immensely wealthy. In his letter, Augustine mentions the “holy widows and virgins that are settled in peace under your (i.e. Proba’s) care” and he adds, “for the more pious the manner in which you order your house, the more are you bound to persevere fervently in prayer, not engaging yourselves with the affairs of this world further than is demanded in the interests of religion” (Letter 130 16.30).[9]

Female Patrons and Abbesses

There were many women in the early church, like Marcella, Macrina, and Grapte, mentioned in part 3, and like Tabitha, Gavia, and Proba: godly, intelligent, and wealthy women who were patrons, and often also teachers, of widows and virgins. And many of these women also housed single women.

In the fourth century, Olympias, who was an ordained deaconess, built a huge monastery that housed 250 celibate deaconesses. Some wealthy women, such as Macrina, Paula, Melania, and Marthana, founded and led double monasteries for single celibate women and men.[10] Permanent celibacy was not a fringe expression of Christianity in early Christianity.

The Rise and Fall of Widows and Virgins as Church Orders

When we read the section about widows in 1 Timothy 5, we shouldn’t assume that all, or even most, of these women were needy or marginalised. The enrolled Widows were equivalent to, or part of, the elders who are mentioned immediately before and after the passage on widows (1 Tim. 5:1-2; 17-20). And the younger widows of Ephesus were probably like the virgin-widows of Smyrna who held a usually respected place in early Christian congregations. These single women had status in the Christian community. (I’ve discussed the status and authority of celibate women in part 3.)

The status of enrolled Widows grew after the first century. Bonnie Thurston states that in the third century, Widows “reached their highest official position in the hierarchy of the church.”[11] and that the beginning of the third century was “the era of their greatest influence.”[12] Accordingly, Lisa Moore writes that “The Widow evolves from someone who is pitied in the Old Testament into an authoritative figure who is to be emulated in the early Church.”[13]

Christine Schenk has noted that communities of virgin-widows developed into centres “of evangelization and hubs of female leadership.”[14] Some were also centres of education and promoted literacy. In Syria, choirs of virgins, led by women such as Publia, a widow, were influential in promoting orthodox theology.[15]

However, as the church continued to reinforce a hierarchy of male leadership, especially when it came to liturgical ministry, female clergy were phased out, and women were increasingly denied ecclesial roles. As a result, the office of Widow, and also of deaconess, declined after the fourth century, especially in the Latin-speaking West. Nevertheless, women were still able to devote themselves to Christian service by joining monasteries and convents.

Final Comments

1 Timothy 5:3-16, with its different kinds of widows, can be difficult to follow, but I hope this 5-part article makes this passage easier to understand.

To summarise, in this series on 1 Timothy 5:3-16, I’ve discussed the following groups of single women in the Ephesian church:

  • Genuine widows who, if they needed support, were to be cared for by their relatives or, failing that, the church.
  • Enrolled Widows, older women of exemplary character who had made a pledge, who were recognised as ministers, and who were part of the leadership structure of the Ephesian church.
  • Younger single celibate women, a number of whom were being led astray and leading others astray.
  • Female patrons who cared for some of these women.

Paul addresses issues regarding these women, especially the younger women who were causing problems, but he begins and ends the passage emphasising that real widows be cared for. For these widows, there are no age restrictions or marital qualifications other than genuine widowhood.

To further clarify, the way I understand Paul’s instructions is that he wanted real widows with family to be cared for by relatives, single celibate women were to be cared for by female patrons, and the church would care for real widows who had no family, and possibly the enrolled Widows too, if they needed it.

Footnotes

[1] There is a textual variant in early manuscripts of 1 Timothy 5:16. Instead of just pistē (“a faithful/ believing woman”), many manuscripts have pistos ē pistē  (“a faithful/ believing man or woman”). The NET Bible has a useful note on this.

Most witnesses (D Ψ 1175 1241 1505 M al sy) have πιστὸς ἤ (pistos ē) before πιστή (pistē), with the resultant meaning “if a believing man or woman.” But such looks to be a motivated reading, perhaps to bring some parity to the responsibilities of men and women listed here, and as a way of harmonizing with v. 4. Further, most of the earlier and better witnesses (א A C F G P 048 33 81 1739 1881 co) lack the πιστὸς ἤ, strengthening the preference for the shorter reading. (NETBible.org, note 26 on 1 Timothy 5)

The shorter reading seems to be original and is what most English translations have adopted. For example, the NIV has, “If any woman who is a believer has widows …”  The KJV, however, has “If any man or woman that believeth have widows …” (My use of italics.)

[2] Some patrons of widows would have been men. The Acts of Peter contains a brief account of a man named Marcellus. According to the story, Marcellus was a Roman senator, a Christian, and a generous patron of the poor. The story includes this piece of dialogue.

“Believe us, brother Peter,” they said, “none among men was so wise as this Marcellus. All widows, who hoped in Christ, took their refuge in him; all orphans were fed by him. Will you know more, brother? All the poor called Marcellus their patron; his house was called the house of the pilgrims and poor.”
Acts of Peter 8. (Internet Archive p. 71)

The Acts of Peter is a work of fiction which was written in the second half of the second century. Nevertheless, it indicates what some early Christian patrons did, including protecting poor widows.

[3] Christine Trevett notes that we have evidence that women in the early church helped “by sheltering the ascetically inclined who were separated from their own unsympathetic families.”
Trevett, Christian Women and the Time of the Apostolic Fathers (AD c.80-160): Corinth, Rome and Asia Minor (University of Wales Press, 2006), 219.

[4] The Greek verb poieō translated as “made” in Acts 9:39, referring to the clothing that Tabitha produced “while being with the widows,” has a range of senses. Perhaps the widows, under Tabitha’s leadership and patronage, manufactured clothing as an enterprise.

[5] Thurston, The Widows: A Women’s Ministry in the Early Church (Fortress, 1989), 34. (Internet Archive)

[6] Christine Trevett, Christian Women and the Time of the Apostolic Fathers (AD c.80-160): Corinth, Rome and Asia Minor (University of Wales Press, 2006), 219.

[7] Trevett, Christian Women, 220.

[8] Adolf von Harnack, a respected historian of the early church, associated both Gavia and another prominent woman in the Smyrnaean church, Alke, with the “elect lady,” a woman identified as the recipient of 2 John. Harnack, The Expansion of Christianity in the First Three Centuries, Vol. 2, translated by James Moffatt (Wipf and Stock, 1998), 223-224. Originally published in German in 1902.
I’ve written about Harnack’s views on New Testament women, as well as Gavia and Alke, here.

Clement of Alexandria presumed that “she who is in Babylon,” a woman mentioned at the end of 2 Peter, was one and the same as the “elect lady.” Furthermore, he believed that this woman was the leader of a group of virgins. In his notes on 2 John, Clement wrote, “The second Epistle of John, which is written to virgins, is very simple. It was written to a Babylonian lady, by name Electa …” (Clement, Fragments 4)

Clement’s interpretation of 2 Peter 5:13 and 2 John 1:1 & 5 reflects his own experience of church life, where it was common to have groups of women who had chosen life-long celibacy and who were cared for by a wealthy woman. However, the Greek grammar of 2 John seems to rule out that the elect lady only had female virgins in her congregation. I’ve written about the “elect lady” in 2 John here. I’ve written about “she who is in Babylon here.

[9] In Letter 150, written in 413, Augustine praises Proba because her daughter Julia had consecrated her life as a virgin in the service of Christ.

[10] In later centuries also, women founded and led double monasteries. These women include Brigid of Kildare, Ireland (c. 451–523), Hilda of Whitby, England (c. 614–680), and Etheldreda of Northumbria (c. 636–679). Double monasteries were banned by the Second Council of Nicaea in 787. (Wikipedia) But most of the powerful men and women who ran these establishments didn’t quickly abandon them. The pressure of later reforms and rulings, as well as raids by Vikings and barbarians, led to their demise.

[11] Thurston, The Widows: A Women’s Ministry in the Early Church (Fortress, 1989), 79.

[12] Ibid, 89.

[13] Moore, Widow as the Altar of God, 6.

[14] Schenk, “Honor the ‘mothers’ of early Christianity during Women’s History Month,” National Catholic Reporter (March 2021).

[15] Theodoret of Cyrrhus, Church History 3.14. I’ve written about Publia, a brave and formidable woman, here.

  2. Nancy Young
    August 17, 2026

    Thank you, Marg, for a great article on an important topic. I’m wondering about needy widows in Ephesus who were not Christians. Were they cared for by anyone — was there refuge for them in the Artemis temple, perhaps?

    Reply
    1. Marg
      August 18, 2026

      Hi Nancy, Greco-Roman religions were all about sacrifices, ceremonies, and rituals. They did not usually involve any kind of social welfare on a regular basis.

      There were some legal protections for widows. There were laws about widows receiving their dowry, and by both custom and law, families were obligated to care for widows who needed it. This is one reason why Paul says that someone who does not care for needy widows in their family is worse than an unbeliever (1 Tim. 5:8).

      Reply
